Why the USA

Room to explore. Structure to move forward.

The U.S. system offers a wide range of institutions and study formats. The opportunity is valuable, but only when your choices are grounded in fit, cost and a realistic admissions plan.
One Window helps you turn a large set of options into a focused shortlist based on evidence.

Flexible study

Explore majors, minors, electives and interdisciplinary pathways.

Research ecosystem

Learn through labs, faculty projects and work connected to industry.

Campus experience

Access academic support, student clubs and diverse communities.

Choice at every level

Public universities, private colleges, liberal arts institutions and community colleges create different academic and budget pathways.

Academic flexibility

Many undergraduate programmes allow time to explore subjects before declaring a major, while graduate programmes range from professional to research focused.

Learning beyond lectures

Projects, laboratories, campus organisations and eligible practical training can connect classroom learning with real world contexts.

A global classroom

International students study alongside people from varied cultures, industries and academic backgrounds.

Universities & courses

Find the kind of institution where you can do your best work.

The right university is the one that fits your academic profile, budget, learning style and career direction. Rankings are one input, not the entire decision.

Research universities

Broad programme choice, advanced facilities and strong research activity.

Liberal arts colleges

Smaller undergraduate communities with interdisciplinary learning and close faculty interaction.

Public universities

Large campuses and wide course portfolios; international tuition varies by institution.

Community colleges

Two year programmes that can offer a more affordable route before transferring to a four year institution.

Eligibility

Requirements vary by programme. Prepare the common building blocks early.

Always verify the official international admissions page for each programme. Test policies, score expectations and document formats can change by university and intake.
01

Academic record

Secondary school credentials for undergraduate study or a recognised bachelor’s degree for postgraduate study. Required grades and prerequisites differ by programme.

02

English proficiency

Universities may accept tests such as TOEFL, IELTS, PTE or Duolingo English Test. Minimum scores and waiver rules vary.

03

Standardised tests

SAT, ACT, GRE or GMAT policies vary by institution. Many programmes make tests optional, while others still require or recommend scores.

04

Application materials

Transcripts, recommendations, essays or statements, a résumé for some programmes, and portfolios or prerequisites for selected courses.

Application process

A clear sequence makes a complex application manageable.

Start early, work backwards from each deadline and keep one reliable record of requirements, documents and decisions.
01

Define your direction

Clarify course interests, preferred locations, budget and intake.

02

Build a balanced shortlist

Compare curriculum, outcomes, requirements, total cost and campus fit.

03

Prepare your evidence

Arrange transcripts, test scores, recommendations, essays and financial documents.

04

Submit with control

Track university portals, document requests, interviews and individual deadlines.

05

Evaluate decisions

Compare offers, funding, conditions, programme fit and total cost before committing.

06

Prepare for your visa

After accepting an offer, work through the I-20, SEVIS and F-1 process.

Cost of study

Plan the full cost of attendance, not only tuition.

These figures are planning references, not quotes. Your actual budget depends on institution, programme, location, housing and lifestyle. Use every university’s published cost of attendance before making a decision.
Public four year tuition & fees$9,800 average

NCES 2022 to 2023 public institution average; international rates are often higher than local resident rates.

Private nonprofit tuition & fees$40,700 average

NCES 2022 to 2023 private nonprofit average before institutional aid.

Housing, food & daily livingVaries widely

City, accommodation type, transport and personal spending materially change the budget.

Health insurance, books & feesPlan separately

University insurance, programme fees, supplies and travel may sit outside headline tuition.

NCES averages describe U.S. institutions broadly. International tuition and individual university budgets can differ significantly.

Scholarships & aid

Build funding research into your shortlist from the start.

Funding is competitive and often partial. Admission and financial aid requirements may have different documents and deadlines.

University merit awards

Often linked to academic strength, leadership, talent or the overall application.

Aid based on financial need

Available at some institutions; policies for international applicants differ substantially.

Department and graduate funding

Assistantships, fellowships or tuition support may exist for eligible graduate students.

External scholarships

Foundations, trusts, employers and professional bodies may support specific subjects or applicant groups.

Student visa

The F-1 process starts after an eligible university admits you.

Requirements, fees and appointment availability can change. Follow the U.S. Department of State, your embassy or consulate, SEVP and your university’s Designated School Official.
  1. Receive admission from an institution approved by SEVP and obtain Form I-20.
  2. Pay the required SEVIS I-901 fee and keep the receipt.
  3. Complete the DS-160 nonimmigrant visa application accurately.
  4. Pay the applicable visa application fee and schedule the interview.
  5. Prepare your passport, I-20, DS-160 confirmation, academic records and funding evidence.
  6. Attend the interview. A visa permits travel to a U.S. port of entry; admission is decided by CBP.
Check official student visa guidance
Current official referenceThe listed F/M visa application fee is US$185.

Verify the current visa and SEVIS fees before paying. A visa does not guarantee admission at the port of entry.

Intakes & deadlines

Choose the intake that matches your preparation, not only the calendar.

Fall · August to September

The broadest programme choice. Many undergraduate deadlines fall between November and January for the following academic year.

Spring · Jan

A useful alternative for selected universities and programmes; availability and funding may be narrower.

Summer · May to June

More common for selected courses, pathway programmes and short term study than for full degree entry.

Student life

Plan for the experience around the classroom, too.

Where you live

Choose among residence halls, shared apartments, homestays and private rentals based on campus rules and budget.

How you settle in

International offices, academic advisers, writing centres, health services and student clubs can support the transition.

What to budget for

Plan for deposits, utilities, local transport, phone service, winter clothing and travel, not only rent and food.

Career opportunities

Understand practical training as regulated authorisation, not a job promise.

Internships and training after graduation depend on your status, programme, timing and authorisation. Speak with the university DSO before accepting work or training.

Campus and curricular experience

Eligible students may explore work on campus or authorised Curricular Practical Training where it forms part of the curriculum. Rules must be confirmed with the university DSO.

Optional Practical Training

Eligible F-1 students may apply for temporary work authorisation related to their field of study. Approval is not automatic and students must follow USCIS and SEVP requirements.

STEM OPT extension

Qualifying graduates with eligible STEM degrees may be able to seek a 24 month extension after completing OPT, subject to current rules and employer requirements.

FAQs

Questions students and families ask before applying.

When should I start planning for the USA?+

Ideally 12 to 18 months before your intended intake. This gives you time for research, tests if required, essays, recommendations, funding and visa preparation.

Do all U.S. universities require the SAT, GRE or GMAT?+

No. Testing policies vary by university, programme and intake. Check the official admissions page for every programme on your shortlist.

Can international students receive scholarships?+

Yes, but availability and award size vary. Some universities offer merit awards, some offer aid based on financial need, and graduate departments may offer assistantships or fellowships.

How much money should my family plan for?+

Use each university’s published cost of attendance, not tuition alone. Include housing, meals, insurance, books, travel, visa costs and a sensible contingency.

Does an F-1 visa guarantee entry or employment?+

No. A visa allows you to seek entry at a U.S. port of entry, and CBP makes the admission decision. Employment and practical training require separate eligibility and authorisation.

Can One Window help after I receive offers?+

Yes. The team can help you compare programme fit, funding, conditions, documentation and the next steps toward enrolment and visa preparation.
